questions.question: Define economic growth and GDP per capita. Explain why a growth rate of 3% is very different from 1% over a generation.
questions.expected_answer: Economic growth is an increase in the production of goods and services over time, measured by the growth rate of real GDP. GDP per capita is GDP divided by the population, a rough measure of the average standard of living. Growth compounds: at 3% a year output roughly doubles in about 24 years (1,03^24 ≈ 2,03), while at 1% it takes about 70 years (1,01^70 ≈ 2,01). So at 3% living standards can double within one generation; at 1% they barely change, especially if population grows nearly as fast.

questions.question: Explain four ways the national budget can promote economic growth.
questions.expected_answer: Infrastructure spending (roads, rail, ports, electricity, water) lowers the cost of doing business and attracts investment. Spending on education, skills and health builds human capital and raises productivity. Government spending adds to total demand and has a multiplier effect, and fiscal policy can support demand in a slowdown. Tax incentives (investment allowances, special economic zones, the employment tax incentive) encourage investment and hiring. Controlling the deficit and debt maintains confidence and keeps interest rates lower.

questions.question: Define inequality and the Gini coefficient. Explain how the budget redresses inequality through both revenue and expenditure, and why growth is also needed.
questions.expected_answer: Inequality is an uneven distribution of income or wealth among people. The Gini coefficient measures it from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has all income); South Africa's is about 0,63. Revenue: progressive income tax, taxes on wealth (capital gains, dividends, estate duty), zero-rating basic foods. Expenditure: social grants, the social wage (no-fee schools, school meals, free primary health care, housing, free basic services), and spending on causes such as education, NSFAS, land reform, small business support and public employment programmes. Growth is needed because it creates jobs, the most lasting route out of poverty, and provides the revenue that redistribution depends on.
